title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
hookLine: two sad travelers walk seven miles with a stranger and know him when he breaks bread

lines: THE WALK HOME AFTER BAD NEWS.
cards: After bad news, the walk home goes over it and over it. What happened. What should have happened.
What it all means now. The same Sunday, Luke says, two followers of Jesus are walking away from Jerusalem, toward a village called Emmaus, threescore furlongs off, about seven miles.
One is Cleopas; the other, Luke never names. They're talking it all over: the arrest, the cross, and a strange report from some women about an empty tomb. And a stranger falls into step beside them.

teach.b: Luke tells us who it is, in the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him." He asks what they're discussing, and they stop, faces sad.
Cleopas says: are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Then this line: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel."
We had hoped. Past tense. The stranger doesn't correct them right away.
Starting with Moses and all the prophets, he explains the scriptures about the Messiah.
At the village he acts as if he's going further, and they stop him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." The hymn Abide with Me borrows that line.
At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them: the same four movements as anamnesis, and the feeding on the hillside.
"And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight."
They say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?"

teach.h: KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.
teach.b: That same hour they walk the whole way back, though the day was far spent, to tell the others how he was known to them in the breaking of bread.

teach.h: DID NOT OUR HEART BURN WITHIN US?
teach.b: Luke's story goes on in a second book, the Acts of the Apostles, and this road is the hinge. The story doesn't end at the tomb; it turns around on a road and keeps going.

how: Many churches read the road to Emmaus in the Easter season, and some hold Emmaus walks on Easter Monday. Christians often speak of meeting Christ in scripture and in the breaking of bread, the two halves of many Sunday services.

o: a village where two travelers knew Jesus at supper
the garden outside Jerusalem where Jesus was buried
a lake town where Peter first left his nets

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: he names Cleopas. the other traveler is never named.
they recognized Jesus as soon as he joined them
their eyes were holden that they should not know him, until he broke the bread.
they walked back to Jerusalem that same hour
they got up and returned to tell the others.

games.q: you've walked seven miles with a stranger who opened the scriptures to you. you reach your village at evening, and he acts as though he's going further. what do you do?
o: urge him: abide with us, for it is toward evening.
games.why: they press him to stay. at the table he breaks the bread, their eyes are opened, and they know him.

practice: Find one we had hoped of your own, a plan that fell through, a door that stayed shut, someone who left, and say it the way the two did: I had hoped.

Then walk back over the last few days, as they looked back over the road, to a moment that warmed you while it happened, a talk, a meal, a kindness, you only noticed afterward. Rest there; if you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Emmaus. A village seven miles from Jerusalem, where two sad travelers recognized the stranger who had walked with them, in the breaking of the bread.

orig.note: Greek: in the breaking of the bread. Luke's phrase for how they knew him, which he uses again in Acts.

carryVoice: Your line: our hearts burned. Tomorrow, the disciple who missed it all. That's seventy-one days.
